Last week we had the chance to share what we do every day with the next generation of submarine engineers. 🌊

On 17-18 November 2026, We joined CONNEXUS 2026 "Limitless Waves", a Campus Training Series at Telkom University, Bandung, as a trainer for 50 participants. They were selected through a strict process from campuses all over Indonesia.

Together with Jaisy Ghiyats Muchtar, we had the honor of representing InfraNexia and ASKALSI (Asosiasi Penyelenggara Sistem Komunikasi Kabel Laut Seluruh Indonesia) as trainers forModule 1.3: Submarine Cable System Architecture, "from the terrestrial network to the seabed".

We split the module into four sessions, one system:
🔹 Part 1, End-to-end architecture: terrestrial backhaul, cable landing station, dry plant and wet plant in one big picture
🔹 Part 2, Wet plant: cable armour, fibre pairs, repeaters and branching units
🔹 Part 3, Dry plant: SLTE, PFE, DWDM, coherent transmission, NMS and COTDR
🔹 Part 4, System integration: capacity, redundancy, protection, open cable and what's next

What made these two days special was the participants' enthusiasm. Hands went up for every question, the questions kept coming in every session. Instead of a one-way lecture, it became a real conversation and discussion between engineers in the field and the next-gen engineers.

For an archipelago of 17,000+ islands, submarine cables are not a niche topic. They are the backbone of our digital economy. Seeing this many next-gen engineers curious about it gives us a lot of hope for the industry.

We are also grateful that our sessions were recognized with the Outstanding Trainer Award. 🏆

Thank you, Telkom University, for the opportunity and the warm welcome, and to the whole CONNEXUS 2026 committee for a well-organized program. We hope this program keep growing and inspires more next-gen engineers to join the subsea and backbone industry. 🙏

To the all participants: what's the one thing you'll remember from these two days? 👇

𝗦𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗶𝗼𝘂𝘀! 𝗦𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴! Exploring how power systems, data science, and sustainability collide led me to build Proof of Green. Rachael Ayo-Olalusi inspired this one! 😂  

As an Electrical Engineer master student atInstitut Teknologi Bandung passionate about renewable energy, I wanted to see how one can objectively verify and value clean power without heavy auditing overhead. It is an early stage showcase on the Polygon Amoy testnet without live SCADA access, I got creative and built this. The end-to-end pipeline is now connected, and running. Is "digital twin" fair here? 🤔 Without live plant telemetry, I recreatedPT PLN Nusantara Power's 192 MWp Cirata Floating Solar Plant as a Weather-Driven PV Digital Twin: hourly irradiance and temperature coming from the Open-Meteo historical API (ERA5-based, global, free for non-commercial use), run through a PV model with fixed plant parameters from google, and scored against NASA POWER as an independent check. (A full live-telemetry twin would sync real-time meter/inverter feeds at this stage)  Analyzing output from 9th Nov 2023, the plant inception date to 1st Sept 2026, refreshed daily with a few days' lag:

• Twin generation: 817,489,085 kWh
• NASA-expected generation: 748,569,057 kWh
• Verified energy: 720,762 MWh
• Assumed CO₂ offset: 571,565 tonnes (0.793 kg CO₂/kWh, Indonesia grid average)
• NFTs minted: 0. With the pipeline connected; minting set to quarterly, historically and 1 NFT per 50,000 MWh / 50 GWh forward, should be about 10–11 NFTs lol. Still debugging testnet gas execution, and every failure point is a real-world lesson in Web3 + data pipelines for me.   

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝗶𝗽𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀:
𝟭. 𝗪𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿-𝘁𝗼-𝗣𝗩 𝗧𝘄𝗶𝗻: Pull Open-Meteo ERA5 hourly irradiance & temperature and convert via PV model parameters into simulated output.
𝟮. 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗖𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸: Cross-check against NASA POWER to score validation and flag invalid days.
𝟯. 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗮𝗹 𝗠𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴: Map verified energy to quarterly historical mints and 50,000 MWh (50 GWh) forward NFTs on Polygon tunable to smaller MWh/kWh steps for compact assets. 

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗜𝘁 𝗠𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗚𝗹𝗼𝗯𝗮𝗹 𝗦𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗵 & 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁𝘂𝗽𝘀:
Developing markets face steep clean-energy financing gaps, and traditional MRV can eat into project value. For small solar microgrid operators and startups, lightweight satellite-backed validation and automated on-chain certificates help build trust and unlock green finance. Canva stopped posting jobs months before it restructured 22% of its staff
  
Canva stopped posting jobs before it restructured 22% of staff. Active postings fell 88% from the Feb 23, 2026 peak to Nov 2, 2026.
  
On Nov 3, Canva CEO Melanie Perkins told staff that 1,271 people, about 22% of the company, would lose their jobs, change roles or relocate to central hubs. The company has not disclosed the split between those three groups. Product, Growth and Platform are merging into one product organization, management layers are being removed, and Sydney becomes the primary home for more product teams. Perkins called it the hardest moment in the company's 13 year history, and said growth slowed in 2026 for the first time in a decade. In August Canva cut its 2026 revenue growth forecast from 30% to 20%, according to Business Insider.
  
That is the announcement. The workforce data says the hiring side of Canva turned months earlier, and that the company was still adding people, and managers, right up to the month before.
  
Job postings rolled over in the spring

Revelio Labs tracks Canva's active job postings weekly. They peaked at 3,937 in the week of Nov 3, 2025, after a surge that began the week of Sep 22, 2025. They recovered to a 2026 high of 2,496 in the week of Feb 23. By the week of Jun 22 they were at 1,504. By the week of Nov 2, 2026, the last week before the announcement, they were at 311.
  
That is a drop of 88% from the 2026 high and 79% from the Jun 22 level. Against the same week a year earlier, it is down 92%.
  
Two cautions. The weekly series is noisy, which is why the chart also shows a 4 week average. And the most recent weeks of posting data can be revised as postings are reclassified, so I would read the final reading as directional, not exact. The decline itself, from Feb through Oct, is not a single week artifact.
  
Headcount was still rising in October
  
Our modeled view of Canva's workforce went from 15,588 in Sep 2025 to 16,902 in Oct 2026, up 8.4%. Our modeled count runs well above the roughly 5,800 people implied by Canva's own 1,271 and 22% figures, so the percentages are the signal here, not the level.
  
The flow rates tell a more mixed story. All rates are trailing 12 months:
  
Hiring rate: 37.5% in Dec 2023, down to a trough of 26.1% in Aug 2025, back up to 31.6% in Oct 2026
Attrition rate: 22.1% in Sep 2024, up to 24.5% in Oct 2026
Net growth rate (hires minus exits): 15.9% in Dec 2023, 2.8% in Aug 2025, 7.2% in Oct 2026
  
The hiring rate rising while postings collapsed is not a contradiction. A trailing 12 month rate lags a weekly postings series by months. Postings are the earlier signal. The rate will show the slowdown later.
  
The management layer grew faster than the company
  
Canva said it is removing management layers. The data shows that layer grew faster than the rest of the company over the last 13 months.
  
Change in modeled headcount by seniority, Sep 2025 to Oct 2026:
  
Associate: up 22.7%
Director: up 17.7% 
Executive: up 14.8%
Manager: up 13.4% 
Entry level: up 3.0% 
Junior: down 2.9% 
  
Combine Manager, Director, Executive and Senior Executive into one layer. It went up 14.9%, against 8.1% growth for all staff with a classified seniority. That layer accounted for 37.6% of net headcount growth while representing 20.5% of the starting base. Its share of the workforce moved from 20.5% to 21.8%.
  
Our proxy for span of control, non-managers per person at manager level and above, moved from 3.87 to 3.58, a decline of 7.4%. Revelio does not observe reporting lines, so this is a proxy for organizational depth, not a count of layers.
  
Engineers and sales were the growth, design was flat
  
Change in modeled headcount by role, Sep 2025 to Oct 2026:
  
Software engineering: up 34.8% 
Research engineer: up 34.7% 
Account executive: up 20.9%
Digital marketer: up 15.4% 
Designer: up 3.9%
Web developer: down 3.9%
UX designer: down 5.0%
  
Designers are still the largest role family at about 35% of the company, but that share slipped from 36.9% to 35.4% while software engineering rose from 8.2% to 10.2%. For a company best known as a design tool, the build out of the last year was engineering and research, which fits the stated goal of building AI products.
  
Where the people are
  
Change in modeled headcount by country, Sep 2025 to Oct 2026:
  
United Kingdom: up 27.3% 
United States: up 13.9% 
Australia: up 9.6% 
Indonesia: up 7.9% 
India: down 2.1% 
Philippines: down 9.7%
  
The Philippines peaked in Jan 2026 and has fallen 10.0% since. Australia is 28.9% of the modeled workforce, close to where it started the period. Canva said product teams will concentrate in Sydney, so the geography of the 1,271 relocations and role changes is worth watching in the next few months of data.
  
What employees were already saying
  
Employee sentiment is a percentile rank against the broader dataset, built from the trailing 12 months of reviews. From Jan 2024 to Oct 2026:
  
Overall: 51 to 45
Leadership: 52 to 36
Business outlook: 50 to 39
Job security: 48 to 38
  
Leadership took the largest fall, 16 points. Review volume in the window also declined over this period, from 319 to 184, so the latest readings rest on a thinner base.
  
The talent trade
  
Over the 12 months through Oct 2026, Revelio tracked about 2,400 moves into Canva from other companies and about 1,400 out, roughly 1.7 in for every 1 out. The largest sources were Atlassian (70 in, 8 out) and Amazon (60 in, 10 out), then Microsoft and Alphabet. The largest destinations were Meta (18), Fiverr (17) and Alphabet (14). These are tracked company to company moves, and the counts for individual companies are small.
  
What I would watch next
  
Postings. Whether they stay near 300 or rebuild around the new product org. A restructuring with a hiring reset looks different from one followed by a rebuild in engineering and AI roles.
The management layer. Canva has said layers are coming out. The data to watch is whether the 3.58 non-managers per manager proxy rises back toward 3.87.
Attrition. At 24.5% before the announcement, with a 6 month severance package and the vesting cliff waived for recent hires, the survivors' exit rate in the next 2 to 3 months is the measure of how the reorganization landed.
Geography. Whether Sydney grows and the Philippines and India continue to shrink.
The split. Canva has not said how many of the 1,271 are exits versus role changes or relocations. The headcount series from Nov 2026 onward is where that will show.

What this is and is not. This is not a story about a company that was shrinking. Through Oct 2026 Canva's modeled workforce was still growing, and it was adding engineers, researchers and managers. It is a story about the sequence: the demand signal turned in the spring, the announcement came in November, and the headcount data that would confirm the cut has not yet arrived.

Two questions follow each person we place, long after their start date.

Do they have a good job? And are they doing a good job?

That’s how we describe what matters once someone starts with a client.

One is about the person and how the role is working for them day to day.

The other is about the client and whether the hire is giving the team what it needs.

And they’re both interlinked. 

Picture a cloud engineer six weeks into a 12-month project. The client is pleased with the work. The engineer has also been logging on most evenings and answering messages on weekends to keep up.

On paper, they’re doing a good job. Whether it still feels like a good job by month four is harder to say.

A conversation at this point gives both sides time to adjust. Changes can be made while the project still has 10 months to run. The client also keeps an engineer who wants to stay.

We aim to have these conversations early, with the people we place and the teams they join. It’s the same approach we’re bringing to every region that we work in, from the US to Indonesia. 

If a new technical hire or team is on the plan for 2027, send us a message. We’re happy to talk through how we support both sides once someone starts.

Your overseas data centers just inherited a US export compliance nightmare.

The Commerce Department just issued an interim final rule requiring export licenses for advanced AI chips sent to facilities in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil if they remotely serve Chinese entities.

The policy goal is clear: close the remote cloud leasing loophole.

The operational reality is an identity verification problem.

Hardware export controls were built around tracking physical silicon. You verify physical shipments before they cross a border.

Policing remote compute across borders is a software identity problem.

On raw network traffic, an engineer in Shanghai leasing remote GPU clusters in Johor or Singapore looks identical to any standard enterprise user. Network traffic alone does not reveal who is behind the connection.

Data center operators run infrastructure.

They are not equipped to police end-user nationality.

Washington wants global cloud providers and colocation operators to police end-user nationality at the server level.

The physical silicon stays in Southeast Asia.

The compliance drag hits every global infrastructure team.

If your company operates remote compute in Asia, who owns end-user verification today: your legal compliance team or your infrastructure engineers?

The Drill-Down from Sorot Energi explains one oil and gas term in about a minute. Today: the recovery factor.

What it means: the share of a field's original oil that is produced, or expected to be.

Why oil stays behind: oil sits in tiny spaces between grains of rock. At first, the field's own pressure pushes it to the wells. As that pressure drops, the flow slows, and some oil gets stuck in the narrowest gaps. Thick, heavy oil moves even less.

Indonesia's example is Duri, in the Rokan block in Riau. Its oil is heavy. Without help, only about 7 to 8% of it was expected to come out. In 1985, Caltex began pumping steam into the field to heat and thin the oil. With steam, engineers expected about 60%. In 2022, the Directorate General of Oil and Gas put it above 70%.

The work continues. Pertamina Hulu Rokan, the operator since 2021, started steam in a new area, North Duri Area 14, in January 2025.

The catch: steam has to be made, and that takes fuel. In 1990, about a fifth of Duri's oil was expected to be burned to make steam, unless more gas was found.

Key term: recovery factor = how much of a field's original oil comes out.

Your Next Career Move Starts Before You're Ready

Looking back at my career journey, from starting as a Storage Engineer at Fujitsu to becoming Country Director at Veeam, one thing has remained constant: the willingness to keep learning and embrace new challenges. 

My leadership journey began at Dimension Data, followed by VMware in 2020, where I led the Solutions Engineering team before eventually becoming Country Manager for VMware Indonesia. In 2026, I took another leap, joining Veeam to build its presence in Indonesia. 

It wasn't something I had planned from day one. But I've learned that career growth isn't just about becoming better at what you do. It's about expanding what you're capable of taking responsibility for. 

Here are three lessons that have shaped my journey: 

1. Never stop learning beyond your current role.
Technical expertise may open doors, but understanding the business, the market, and the bigger picture is what helps you grow. 

2. Don't wait until you're ready to take on responsibility.
Growth often comes from stepping into unfamiliar situations. You won't always have the answers, but the willingness to learn, make decisions, and be accountable will take you further. 

3. Leadership is about people, not positions.
Success becomes less about individual achievements and more about empowering others, building trust, and bringing people together toward a common goal. 

Don't just work towards your next title. Work towards becoming someone ready for the responsibility that comes with it. 

What's that lesson that has shaped your own career journey? I'd love to hear your thoughts and experiences in the comments. Don't also forget to share this to those in or preparing for a leadership position!

A lot of you ask me how to figure out what to post on LinkedIn. I spent 2 hours in a LinkedIn masterclass by THE Lara Acosta on a Sunday night, so you don’t have to 😂 

If you don’t know Lara, she made Forbes 30 Under 30 list, built 7-figure businesses onLinkedIn and helped 5,000+ people build their personal brands. I mean, what a role model, right??

Now, let me spill the tea for you 👀🍵

The idea: your unfair advantage sits where these three overlap.
1/ Scars. What you overcame.
2/ Skills. What's easy for you, hard for everyone else.
3/ Proof. What you can actually show for it.

I did the exercise live, on myself. Here's what came out.

🙃 Scars: What have you been through that changed how you do things?
- I moved from Jakarta, Indonesia to Bonn, Germany without speaking any German and had to rebuild my network from the ground up. 
- Almost got unemployed after 2.5 years in the same corporation despite having worked across 4 teams, 2 job functions across 2 countries where I constantly have to prove myself each time.
-Recently, I found myself as the non-technical PM in a room full of AI engineers and architects. 

🤝 Skills: What comes naturally to you that other people find hard?
For me, it’s connecting with strangers (which is really friends waiting to happen), building with AI, translating technical concepts into business impact, embracing change (never thought about how handy this actually is), and connecting dots between things that don’t obviously go together. 
And writing on LinkedIn, not Lara-level yet, but I'll get there ☺️

🏅 Proof: What can you actually show for it?
I've turned coffee chats into jobs, LinkedIn cold outreaches into speaking opportunities, and a coworking space chat into real friendship (this one I'm most proud of).
I built a web app from scratch that got 183 visits in 2 weeks. 
I wrote a post that got over 17,000 impressions.

Doing this exercise out loud made me realize my actual story was never about AI or the tools I use. It's about sharing the things only I've experienced and how it shaped my thinking and my career path.

This is 1 of 3 frameworks I took from the masterclass that felt useful to me as a Gen Z woman in tech working in corporate. Thank YOU for the immense knowledge-sharing session,Lara! YOU ROCK!! 👏

Canva stopped posting jobs months before it restructured 22% of its staff
  
Canva stopped posting jobs before it restructured 22% of staff. Active postings fell 88% from the Feb 23, 2026 peak to Nov 2, 2026.
  
On Nov 3, Canva CEO Melanie Perkins told staff that 1,271 people, about 22% of the company, would lose their jobs, change roles or relocate to central hubs. The company has not disclosed the split between those three groups. Product, Growth and Platform are merging into one product organization, management layers are being removed, and Sydney becomes the primary home for more product teams. Perkins called it the hardest moment in the company's 13 year history, and said growth slowed in 2026 for the first time in a decade. In August Canva cut its 2026 revenue growth forecast from 30% to 20%, according to Business Insider.
  
That is the announcement. The workforce data says the hiring side of Canva turned months earlier, and that the company was still adding people, and managers, right up to the month before.
  
Job postings rolled over in the spring

Revelio Labs tracks Canva's active job postings weekly. They peaked at 3,937 in the week of Nov 3, 2025, after a surge that began the week of Sep 22, 2025. They recovered to a 2026 high of 2,496 in the week of Feb 23. By the week of Jun 22 they were at 1,504. By the week of Nov 2, 2026, the last week before the announcement, they were at 311.
  
That is a drop of 88% from the 2026 high and 79% from the Jun 22 level. Against the same week a year earlier, it is down 92%.
  
Two cautions. The weekly series is noisy, which is why the chart also shows a 4 week average. And the most recent weeks of posting data can be revised as postings are reclassified, so I would read the final reading as directional, not exact. The decline itself, from Feb through Oct, is not a single week artifact.
  
Headcount was still rising in October
  
Our modeled view of Canva's workforce went from 15,588 in Sep 2025 to 16,902 in Oct 2026, up 8.4%. Our modeled count runs well above the roughly 5,800 people implied by Canva's own 1,271 and 22% figures, so the percentages are the signal here, not the level.
  
The flow rates tell a more mixed story. All rates are trailing 12 months:
  
Hiring rate: 37.5% in Dec 2023, down to a trough of 26.1% in Aug 2025, back up to 31.6% in Oct 2026
Attrition rate: 22.1% in Sep 2024, up to 24.5% in Oct 2026
Net growth rate (hires minus exits): 15.9% in Dec 2023, 2.8% in Aug 2025, 7.2% in Oct 2026
  
The hiring rate rising while postings collapsed is not a contradiction. A trailing 12 month rate lags a weekly postings series by months. Postings are the earlier signal. The rate will show the slowdown later.
  
The management layer grew faster than the company
  
Canva said it is removing management layers. The data shows that layer grew faster than the rest of the company over the last 13 months.
  
Change in modeled headcount by seniority, Sep 2025 to Oct 2026:
  
Associate: up 22.7%
Director: up 17.7% 
Executive: up 14.8%
Manager: up 13.4% 
Entry level: up 3.0% 
Junior: down 2.9% 
  
Combine Manager, Director, Executive and Senior Executive into one layer. It went up 14.9%, against 8.1% growth for all staff with a classified seniority. That layer accounted for 37.6% of net headcount growth while representing 20.5% of the starting base. Its share of the workforce moved from 20.5% to 21.8%.
  
Our proxy for span of control, non-managers per person at manager level and above, moved from 3.87 to 3.58, a decline of 7.4%. Revelio does not observe reporting lines, so this is a proxy for organizational depth, not a count of layers.
  
Engineers and sales were the growth, design was flat
  
Change in modeled headcount by role, Sep 2025 to Oct 2026:
  
Software engineering: up 34.8% 
Research engineer: up 34.7% 
Account executive: up 20.9%
Digital marketer: up 15.4% 
Designer: up 3.9%
Web developer: down 3.9%
UX designer: down 5.0%
  
Designers are still the largest role family at about 35% of the company, but that share slipped from 36.9% to 35.4% while software engineering rose from 8.2% to 10.2%. For a company best known as a design tool, the build out of the last year was engineering and research, which fits the stated goal of building AI products.
  
Where the people are
  
Change in modeled headcount by country, Sep 2025 to Oct 2026:
  
United Kingdom: up 27.3% 
United States: up 13.9% 
Australia: up 9.6% 
Indonesia: up 7.9% 
India: down 2.1% 
Philippines: down 9.7%
  
The Philippines peaked in Jan 2026 and has fallen 10.0% since. Australia is 28.9% of the modeled workforce, close to where it started the period. Canva said product teams will concentrate in Sydney, so the geography of the 1,271 relocations and role changes is worth watching in the next few months of data.
  
What employees were already saying
  
Employee sentiment is a percentile rank against the broader dataset, built from the trailing 12 months of reviews. From Jan 2024 to Oct 2026:
  
Overall: 51 to 45
Leadership: 52 to 36
Business outlook: 50 to 39
Job security: 48 to 38
  
Leadership took the largest fall, 16 points. Review volume in the window also declined over this period, from 319 to 184, so the latest readings rest on a thinner base.
  
The talent trade
  
Over the 12 months through Oct 2026, Revelio tracked about 2,400 moves into Canva from other companies and about 1,400 out, roughly 1.7 in for every 1 out. The largest sources were Atlassian (70 in, 8 out) and Amazon (60 in, 10 out), then Microsoft and Alphabet. The largest destinations were Meta (18), Fiverr (17) and Alphabet (14). These are tracked company to company moves, and the counts for individual companies are small.
  
What I would watch next
  
Postings. Whether they stay near 300 or rebuild around the new product org. A restructuring with a hiring reset looks different from one followed by a rebuild in engineering and AI roles.
The management layer. Canva has said layers are coming out. The data to watch is whether the 3.58 non-managers per manager proxy rises back toward 3.87.
Attrition. At 24.5% before the announcement, with a 6 month severance package and the vesting cliff waived for recent hires, the survivors' exit rate in the next 2 to 3 months is the measure of how the reorganization landed.
Geography. Whether Sydney grows and the Philippines and India continue to shrink.
The split. Canva has not said how many of the 1,271 are exits versus role changes or relocations. The headcount series from Nov 2026 onward is where that will show.

What this is and is not. This is not a story about a company that was shrinking. Through Oct 2026 Canva's modeled workforce was still growing, and it was adding engineers, researchers and managers. It is a story about the sequence: the demand signal turned in the spring, the announcement came in November, and the headcount data that would confirm the cut has not yet arrived.

🇮🇩 Indonesia 2027: When Macro Risk Meets Mission-Critical Infrastructure 🏗️

The Rupiah hit a record low of Rp18,270/USD 📉
The JCI dropped to ~5,146 📉
External debt stands at US$458.9B 💸
BI-Rate was raised to 6.00% 🏦

Most people see a warning sign. I see a stress test for national readiness, and a strategic window for the data center industry. 🔍

I recently completed a policy study on Indonesia's readiness for 2027 and its six strategic priorities:
1️⃣ National Readiness & Public Trust
2️⃣ Critical Infrastructure & Secure Mobility
3️⃣ Digital Trust 🔐
4️⃣ Safe Cities
5️⃣ Emergency Readiness
6️⃣ Human Readiness

Three of them point straight at the data center ecosystem: 👇

🔹 Digital Trust – the study calls for decentralized national data centers with automated disaster recovery, cloud sovereignty for strategic data, and 24/7 CSIRTs for finance and energy.

🔹 Critical Infrastructure – energy resilience and secure supply chains are now national-security topics, not just operational ones. ⚡

🔹 Emergency Readiness – business continuity is no longer optional.

Add to that:
👥 ~289M people projected by 2027, 60%+ urban
💳 One of the world's fastest-growing digital payment ecosystems (QRIS, BI-FAST)
🛡️ A maturing data protection regime (UU PDP No. 27/2022)

➡️ Sustained demand for secure, sovereign, resilient digital infrastructure. 🚀

But here's the catch that every procurement and delivery leader should care about: 🎯

With 70%+ of Indonesia's imports being raw materials and capital goods, a weak Rupiah hits data center CAPEX directly. Winners in 2027 will be those who master:

✅ FX-risk-aware sourcing and contracting
✅ Supplier diversification and long-lead-item strategy
✅ Local content and vendor development
✅ Supply chain resilience for power, cooling & critical MEP equipment

💡 My view: in 2027, procurement is a competitive advantage, not a back-office function.

Having been part of three hyperscale data center projects in Indonesia 🏢, I've seen how early sourcing decisions can make or break cost, schedule and uptime.

💬 What's your take: will 2027 slow data center investment in Indonesia, or accelerate the move to resilient, sovereign infrastructure? 👇
